body.sub-school-wellbeing-measures.intro: In recent years, an increasing number of education systems have come to regard student wellbeing as a goal comparable in importance to academic outcomes. International studies include questions on subjective wellbeing, and national and regional monitoring systems are introducing their own indicators.

The diversity of instruments makes it difficult to choose among them and to compare results. The aim of this review is to systematise existing instruments for measuring the subjective wellbeing of schoolchildren and to assess their psychometric quality from the standpoint of their applicability in Russian schools.
body.sub-school-wellbeing-measures.metho: The search was conducted in bibliographic databases on psychology and education for 2000–2025. Publications were included that describe the development or testing of the psychometric properties of a self-report instrument of subjective wellbeing for children and adolescents aged 8–18 years. Of the 1,420 records, 116 publications describing 38 instruments were selected.

The methodological quality of the studies and the psychometric properties were assessed independently by two experts using the COSMIN checklist. For each property, the overall rating was given as “sufficient”, “insufficient” or “indeterminate”.
body.sub-school-wellbeing-measures.resul: The distribution of instruments by theoretical basis and by the presence of a separate school wellbeing component is presented in Table 1. Most instruments are multidimensional and include from three to seven subscales.

The share of instruments with sufficient evidence for each psychometric property is shown in Fig. 1. Reliability and structural validity have been studied most thoroughly, and responsiveness and measurement invariance least.

body.sub-school-wellbeing-measures.discu: The lack of evidence on measurement invariance is the main limitation on the use of the instruments in monitoring, where results are compared across age groups, schools and regions. Without such testing, differences in scores may reflect differences in how the questions are understood rather than real differences in wellbeing.
For Russian schools, full validation of the existing Russian-language versions, including testing of invariance across primary, lower secondary and upper secondary school, is particularly pressing.
body.sub-school-wellbeing-measures.concl: Existing instruments for measuring schoolchildren’s wellbeing are diverse, but their psychometric properties have been studied unevenly. For monitoring purposes, it is recommended to use instruments with confirmed measurement invariance and to continue the validation of the Russian-language versions.
